Endomorphisms of Hecke–Kiselman Monoids Associated to Simple Oriented Graphs

Luka Andrenšek
Abstract

Let HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} denote the Hecke–Kiselman monoid associated to a finite simple oriented graph Θ\Theta. We reduce the problem of describing the endomorphism monoid End⁡(HKΘ)\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}) to determining when a product of two idempotents in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} is again an idempotent. This yields a procedure for constructing a Boolean matrix monoid isomorphic to End⁡(HKΘ)\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}). As an application, we obtain an explicit description of the endomorphism monoid of the Catalan monoid 𝒞n+1\mathcal{C}_{n+1}.

keywords
Hecke–Kiselman monoid, endomorphism monoid, idempotent, Catalan monoid, Boolean matrix monoid

1 Introduction and Main Results

Let Θ=(V,E)\Theta=(V,E) be a finite simple oriented graph, that is, a finite oriented graph with no loops and at most one edge between any two vertices. If there is an arrow from ii to jj, we write i→ji\to j. If there are no arrows i→ji\to j or j→ij\to i and i≠ji\neq j, we say that ii and jj are not connected.

In Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk (2011), Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk define the Hecke–Kiselman monoid HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} associated to Θ\Theta as the monoid generated by idempotents

{xi∣i∈V}\{x_{i}\mid i\in V\}

subject to the following defining relations for all i,j∈Vi,j\in V:

  • •

    xi​xj=xj​xix_{i}x_{j}=x_{j}x_{i} if ii and jj are not connected;

  • •

    xi​xj​xi=xj​xi​xj=xi​xjx_{i}x_{j}x_{i}=x_{j}x_{i}x_{j}=x_{i}x_{j} if i→ji\to j.

We denote by ee the unit element of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}.

Hecke–Kiselman monoids were originally introduced in the setting of simple mixed graphs Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk (2011). They have been studied by various authors Aragona and D’Andrea (2013); Aragona and D’Andrea (2020); Ashikhmin et al. (2015); Collina and D’Andrea (2015); Forsberg (2017); Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk (2011); Lebed (2025); Wiertel (2024). Particular interest has been devoted to the corresponding Hecke–Kiselman algebras Okniński and Wiertel (2020); Okniński (2021); Wiertel (2022); Wiertel (2023).

From the proof of (Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk, 2011, Theorem 16), it follows that every monoid isomorphism φ:HKΘ→HKΘ′\varphi:\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}\to\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta^{\prime}} induces a graph isomorphism fφ:Θ→Θ′f_{\varphi}:\Theta\to\Theta^{\prime} and every graph isomorphism f:Θ→Θ′f:\Theta\to\Theta^{\prime} induces a monoid isomorphism φf:HKΘ→HKΘ′\varphi^{f}:\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}\to\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta^{\prime}}. Setting Θ′=Θ\Theta^{\prime}=\Theta, it can be verified that the automorphism group of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} is isomorphic to the automorphism group of the graph Θ\Theta. To the best of our knowledge, the structure and properties of endomorphisms of Hecke–Kiselman monoids have not been systematically explored.

A description of endomorphisms of the Kiselman monoid D’Andrea and Stella (2023); Kiselman (2002); Kudryavtseva and Mazorchuk (2009), which is the Hecke–Kiselman monoid corresponding to the full acyclic oriented graph, is known in the literature Andrenšek (2025). In this paper, we adapt ideas from Andrenšek (2025) to study the endomorphism monoid of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}.

For a positive integer kk, we denote [k]={1,2,…,k}[k]=\{1,2,\dots,k\}. Throughout the paper, we assume V=[n]V=[n] for some positive integer nn. In Section 2, we define AΘA_{\Theta} to be the set of all subsets X⊆VX\subseteq V such that the full subgraph of Θ\Theta with vertex set XX does not contain any oriented cycles. It is shown that for each X∈AΘX\in A_{\Theta}, there exists a unique idempotent eXe_{X} in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} with content XX.

For X,Y∈AΘX,Y\in A_{\Theta}, we define the predicate p⁡(X,Y)p(X,Y) by

p⁡(X,Y):⇔eX​eY​ is an idempotent in ​HKΘ.p(X,Y):\!\iff e_{X}e_{Y}\text{ is an idempotent in }\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}.

We define (Θ,p)(\Theta,p)-pure sequences of subsets of [n][n] to be sequences (X1,X2,…,Xn)(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}) such that, for all i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n], the following conditions are satisfied:

  1. (i)

    Xi∈AΘX_{i}\in A_{\Theta};

  2. (ii)

    p⁡(Xi,Xj)p(X_{i},X_{j}) and p⁡(Xj,Xi)p(X_{j},X_{i}) hold if ii and jj are not connected;

  3. (iii)

    p⁡(Xi,Xj)p(X_{i},X_{j}) holds if i→ji\to j.

We denote the set of all such sequences by Sn​(Θ,p)S_{n}(\Theta,p). We further define a natural binary operation ∗\ast on Sn​(Θ,p)S_{n}(\Theta,p) and show that it becomes a monoid with this operation.

The main result of this paper is that

End⁡(HKΘ)≅Sn​(Θ,p).\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta})\cong S_{n}(\Theta,p).

Using the characteristic-matrix encoding of such sequences, we then obtain a Boolean matrix monoid isomorphic to End⁡(HKΘ)\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}). Finally, we use this framework to concretely describe all endomorphisms of the Catalan monoid 𝒞n+1\mathcal{C}_{n+1}.

The paper proceeds as follows. In Section 2, we recall some results on Hecke–Kiselman monoids which we use throughout the paper. In Section 3, we present and prove the main result and illustrate it in the case when HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} is isomorphic to the Kiselman monoid. This example is included merely for illustration, since all endomorphisms of the Kiselman monoid are already known in the literature. The paper concludes with Section 4, where we derive an explicit description of all endomorphisms of the Catalan monoid, which is a novel result.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 The Content Map

For a word ww over the alphabet {x1,x2,…,xn}\{x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}\}, we define its content as the set of indices ii for which xix_{i} appears in ww. Since the defining relations of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} preserve content, we can define the content c⁡(x)c(x) for x∈HKΘx\in\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} as the content of any word which represents xx. Moreover, we have

c⁡(x​y)=c⁡(x)∪c⁡(y)andc⁡(e)=∅,c(xy)=c(x)\cup c(y)\quad\text{and}\quad c(e)=\emptyset,

which shows that c:HKΘ→𝟚[n]c:\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}\to\mathbbm{2}^{[n]} is a monoid epimorphism, where 𝟚[n]\mathbbm{2}^{[n]} is equipped with the operation ∪\cup.

We use the following lemma in the proof of Theorem 3.4.

Lemma 2.1.

Let ψ,φ∈End⁡(HKΘ)\psi,\varphi\in\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}). Then

c⁡((ψ∘φ)​(xi))=⋃j∈c⁡(φ⁡(xi))c⁡(ψ⁡(xj)).c((\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i}))=\bigcup_{j\in c(\varphi(x_{i}))}c(\psi(x_{j})).
Proof.

If φ⁡(xi)=e\varphi(x_{i})=e, then we have c⁡(φ⁡(xi))=∅c(\varphi(x_{i}))=\emptyset and (ψ∘φ)​(xi)=e(\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i})=e. Hence c⁡((ψ∘φ)​(xi))=∅c((\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i}))=\emptyset, and thus the conclusion holds in this case.

Now suppose φ⁡(xi)≠e\varphi(x_{i})\neq e and write φ⁡(xi)=xi1​…​xik\varphi(x_{i})=x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{k}} for some k≥1k\geq 1 and i1,…,ik∈Vi_{1},\dots,i_{k}\in V. Then c⁡(φ⁡(xi))={i1,…,ik}c(\varphi(x_{i}))=\{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}\} and we further have

(ψ∘φ)​(xi)=ψ⁡(xi1​…​xik)=ψ⁡(xi1)​…​ψ​(xik).(\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i})=\psi(x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{k}})=\psi(x_{i_{1}})\dots\psi(x_{i_{k}}).

Hence we have

c⁡((ψ∘φ)​(xi))=c⁡(ψ⁡(xi1))∪⋯∪c⁡(ψ⁡(xik)),c((\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i}))=c(\psi(x_{i_{1}}))\cup\dots\cup c(\psi(x_{i_{k}})),

and therefore,

c⁡((ψ∘φ)​(xi))=⋃j∈{i1,…,ik}c⁡(ψ⁡(xj))=⋃j∈c⁡(φ⁡(xi))c⁡(ψ⁡(xj)).c((\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i}))=\bigcup_{j\in\{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}\}}c(\psi(x_{j}))=\bigcup_{j\in c(\varphi(x_{i}))}c(\psi(x_{j})).

∎

2.2 The Kiselman Monoid

This monoid was first introduced in Kiselman (2002) and its later generalisation KnK_{n} was defined in Kudryavtseva and Mazorchuk (2009). It is the monoid given by the following presentation:

Kn=⟨a1,a2,…,an∣ai2=ai,aiajai=ajaiaj=aiaj,i>j⟩.K_{n}=\langle a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}\mid a_{i}^{2}=a_{i},a_{i}a_{j}a_{i}=a_{j}a_{i}a_{j}=a_{i}a_{j},i>j\rangle.

The Kiselman monoid arises as a special case of the HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} monoid. If Θ\Theta is such that i→j⇔i>ji\to j\iff i>j, then HKΘ≅Kn\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}\cong K_{n}.

Let X⊆[n]X\subseteq[n] be nonempty. Write X={i1,i2,…,ik}X=\{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k}\} with i1<i2<⋯<iki_{1}<i_{2}<\dots<i_{k}. We define

ϵX=aik​…​ai2​ai1,\epsilon_{X}=a_{i_{k}}\dots a_{i_{2}}a_{i_{1}},

and also set ϵ∅\epsilon_{\emptyset} to be the unit of KnK_{n}. In (Kudryavtseva and Mazorchuk, 2009, Proposition 11), it is proved that {ϵX∣X⊆[n]}\{\epsilon_{X}\mid X\subseteq[n]\} is the set of all idempotents in KnK_{n}. Note that c⁡(ϵX)=Xc(\epsilon_{X})=X for X⊆[n]X\subseteq[n]. The following is proved in (Kudryavtseva and Mazorchuk, 2009, Proposition 14).

Proposition 2.2.

Let X,Y⊆[n]X,Y\subseteq[n]. Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    ϵX​ϵY\epsilon_{X}\epsilon_{Y} is an idempotent.

  2. (ii)

    ϵX​ϵY=ϵX∪Y\epsilon_{X}\epsilon_{Y}=\epsilon_{X\cup Y}.

  3. (iii)

    For every x∈X∖Yx\in X\setminus Y and every y∈Y∖Xy\in Y\setminus X we have x>yx>y.

Lemma 2.3.

For every X,Y⊆[n]X,Y\subseteq[n], ϵX∪Y​ϵX\epsilon_{X\cup Y}\epsilon_{X} and ϵY​ϵX∪Y\epsilon_{Y}\epsilon_{X\cup Y} are idempotents.

Proof.

Condition (iii) from Proposition 2.2 vacuously holds for the pairs of sets (X∪Y,X)(X\cup Y,X) and (Y,X∪Y)(Y,X\cup Y), since X∖(X∪Y)=∅X\setminus(X\cup Y)=\emptyset and Y∖(X∪Y)=∅Y\setminus(X\cup Y)=\emptyset, from which the claim follows. ∎

2.3 Idempotents in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}

For X⊆VX\subseteq V, denote by Θ⁡[X]\Theta[X] the full subgraph of Θ\Theta with vertex set XX, that is, Θ⁡[X]=(X,E′)\Theta[X]=(X,E^{\prime}) where (i,j)∈E′(i,j)\in E^{\prime} if and only if (i,j)∈E(i,j)\in E and i,j∈Xi,j\in X. Since Θ⁡[X]\Theta[X] is a full subgraph of Θ\Theta, the inclusion Θ⁡[X]↪Θ\Theta[X]\hookrightarrow\Theta induces, by (Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk, 2011, Proposition 15), a monomorphism

HKΘ⁡[X]↪HKΘ.\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta[X]}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}.

We identify HKΘ⁡[X]\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta[X]} with its image in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}. Then HKΘ⁡[X]\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta[X]} is a submonoid of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}.

In (Forsberg, 2017, Theorem 3.6), the following theorem is proved for a general simple oriented graph Θ\Theta.

Theorem 2.4.

There is a bijection between idempotents in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} and full subgraphs of Θ\Theta which do not contain any oriented cycles.

In the proof, an idempotent is mapped to the full subgraph of Θ\Theta whose vertex set is the content of the idempotent. Therefore, for each X⊆VX\subseteq V such that Θ⁡[X]\Theta[X] does not contain any oriented cycles, there exists exactly one idempotent in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} with content XX. We denote this idempotent by eXe_{X}.

We denote the following set

AΘ={X⊆V∣Θ⁡[X]​ does not contain any oriented cycles}.A_{\Theta}=\{X\subseteq V\mid\Theta[X]\text{ does not contain any oriented cycles}\}.

Theorem 2.4 implies the following proposition.

Proposition 2.5.

The set

{eX∣X∈AΘ}\{e_{X}\mid X\in A_{\Theta}\}

is the set of all idempotents in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}.

The idempotent eXe_{X} can be written explicitly. Note that if Θ⁡[X]\Theta[X] does not contain any oriented cycles, then we can write XX as X={i1,i2,…,ik}X=\{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k}\} such that ij→ij′i_{j}\to i_{j^{\prime}} implies j>j′j>j^{\prime}.

Lemma 2.6.

Let X∈AΘX\in A_{\Theta} and write X={i1,i2,…,ik}X=\{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k}\} in any way such that ij→ij′i_{j}\to i_{j^{\prime}} implies j>j′j>j^{\prime}. Then there exists a monoid epimorphism ϕX:Kk→HKΘ⁡[X]\phi_{X}:K_{k}\to\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta[X]} with ϕX​(aj)=xij\phi_{X}(a_{j})=x_{i_{j}} for j=1,2,…,kj=1,2,\dots,k.

Proposition 2.9.

Let X,Y∈AΘX,Y\in A_{\Theta}. Then eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} if and only if X∪Y∈AΘX\cup Y\in A_{\Theta} and eX​eY=eX∪Ye_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}.

Proof.

If X∪Y∈AΘX\cup Y\in A_{\Theta} and eX​eY=eX∪Ye_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}, then eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent by Proposition 2.5. Conversely, if eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent, then by Proposition 2.5, there exists Z∈AΘZ\in A_{\Theta} such that

eX​eY=eZ.e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{Z}.

Taking contents, we get

Z=c⁡(eZ)=c⁡(eX​eY)=c⁡(eX)∪c⁡(eY)=X∪Y.Z=c(e_{Z})=c(e_{X}e_{Y})=c(e_{X})\cup c(e_{Y})=X\cup Y.

Hence X∪Y∈AΘX\cup Y\in A_{\Theta} and eX​eY=eX∪Ye_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}. ∎

Proposition 2.10.

For X,Y∈AΘX,Y\in A_{\Theta}, the product eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} if and only if

eX​eY​eX=eY​eX​eY=eX​eY.e_{X}e_{Y}e_{X}=e_{Y}e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}.
Proof.

If eX​eY​eX=eY​eX​eY=eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y}e_{X}=e_{Y}e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}, then

eX​eY​eX​eY=(eX​eY​eX)​eY=eX​eY​eY=eX​eY,e_{X}e_{Y}e_{X}e_{Y}=(e_{X}e_{Y}e_{X})e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y},

which shows that eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent.

Conversely, suppose eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent. By Proposition 2.9, it follows that X∪Y∈AΘX\cup Y\in A_{\Theta} and

eX​eY=eX∪Y.e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}. (2)

Since X,Y,X∪Y∈AΘX,Y,X\cup Y\in A_{\Theta}, Lemma 2.8 implies that eX∪Y​eXe_{X\cup Y}e_{X} and eY​eX∪Ye_{Y}e_{X\cup Y} are idempotents. By Proposition 2.9, we have

eX∪Y​eX=e(X∪Y)∪X=eX∪YandeY​eX∪Y=eY∪(X∪Y)=eX∪Y.e_{X\cup Y}e_{X}=e_{(X\cup Y)\cup X}=e_{X\cup Y}\quad\text{and}\quad e_{Y}e_{X\cup Y}=e_{Y\cup(X\cup Y)}=e_{X\cup Y}.

Using (2), we conclude that

eX​eY​eX=eY​eX​eY=eX​eY.e_{X}e_{Y}e_{X}=e_{Y}e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X}e_{Y}.

∎

3 The Endomorphism Condition in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}

In this section, we reduce the problem of describing all endomorphisms of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} to determining when a product of two idempotents in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} is again an idempotent. If we have resolved this problem, we can follow the procedure described in this section to obtain a concrete Boolean matrix monoid that is isomorphic to End⁡(HKΘ)\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}).

3.1 (Θ,p)(\Theta,p)-pure Sequences

For X,Y∈AΘX,Y\in A_{\Theta}, we define the predicate p⁡(X,Y)p(X,Y) by

p⁡(X,Y):⇔eX​eY​ is an idempotent in ​HKΘ.p(X,Y):\!\iff e_{X}e_{Y}\text{ is an idempotent in }\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}.

Formally, pp depends on the graph Θ\Theta, but we omit this dependency. For example, if Θ\Theta is the empty graph, then AΘ=𝟚[n]A_{\Theta}=\mathbbm{2}^{[n]} and any product of two idempotents in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} is again an idempotent. Hence p⁡(X,Y)p(X,Y) holds for all X,Y∈AΘX,Y\in A_{\Theta} in this case.

By Proposition 2.9, for all sets X,Y∈AΘX,Y\in A_{\Theta}, we have

p⁡(X,Y)⇔eX​eY​ is an idempotent in ​HKΘ⇔X∪Y∈AΘ​ and ​eX​eY=eX∪Y.p(X,Y)\iff e_{X}e_{Y}\text{ is an idempotent in }\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}\iff X\cup Y\in A_{\Theta}\text{ and }e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}. (3)
Theorem 3.1.

A map φ:{x1,x2,…,xn}→HKΘ\varphi:\{x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}\}\to\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} extends to a monoid endomorphism of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} if and only if there exist sets X1,X2,…,Xn⊆[n]X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}\subseteq[n] such that, for all i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n], the following conditions hold:

  1. (i)

    Xi∈AΘX_{i}\in A_{\Theta};

  2. (ii)

    φ⁡(xi)=eXi\varphi(x_{i})=e_{X_{i}};

  3. (iii)

    p⁡(Xi,Xj)p(X_{i},X_{j}) and p⁡(Xj,Xi)p(X_{j},X_{i}) hold if ii and jj are not connected;

  4. (iv)

    p⁡(Xi,Xj)p(X_{i},X_{j}) holds if i→ji\to j.

Proof.

Assume that the map φ\varphi extends to an endomorphism of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}, which we also denote by φ\varphi. Since a monoid homomorphism maps idempotents to idempotents, φ⁡(xi)\varphi(x_{i}) is an idempotent in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} for all i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\dots,n. By Proposition 2.5, φ⁡(xi)\varphi(x_{i}) is of the form eXe_{X} for some X∈AΘX\in A_{\Theta}. Hence there exist sets X1,X2,…,Xn∈AΘX_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}\in A_{\Theta} such that

φ⁡(xi)=eXi,\varphi(x_{i})=e_{X_{i}},

for all i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\dots,n, which proves (i) and (ii). Now let i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n].

Case 1: ii and jj are not connected. In this case, we have

xi​xj=xj​xi.x_{i}x_{j}=x_{j}x_{i}.

This implies

xi​xj​xi​xj=xi​(xj​xi)​xj=xi​xi​xj​xj=xi​xj.x_{i}x_{j}x_{i}x_{j}=x_{i}(x_{j}x_{i})x_{j}=x_{i}x_{i}x_{j}x_{j}=x_{i}x_{j}.

Hence, xi​xjx_{i}x_{j} is an idempotent. Since φ\varphi maps idempotents to idempotents, it follows that eXi​eXje_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}} is an idempotent, and hence p⁡(Xi,Xj)p(X_{i},X_{j}) holds. Since

eXj​eXi=φ⁡(xj​xi)=φ⁡(xi​xj)=eXi​eXj,e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}}=\varphi(x_{j}x_{i})=\varphi(x_{i}x_{j})=e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}},

we conclude that eXj​eXie_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}} is an idempotent as well, and thus p⁡(Xj,Xi)p(X_{j},X_{i}) also holds. This proves (iii).

Case 2: i→ji\to j. In this case, we have

xi​xj​xi=xj​xi​xj=xi​xj,x_{i}x_{j}x_{i}=x_{j}x_{i}x_{j}=x_{i}x_{j},

and hence

xi​xj​xi​xj=(xi​xj​xi)​xj=xi​xj​xj=xi​xj.x_{i}x_{j}x_{i}x_{j}=(x_{i}x_{j}x_{i})x_{j}=x_{i}x_{j}x_{j}=x_{i}x_{j}.

Therefore, xi​xjx_{i}x_{j} is an idempotent, and by applying φ\varphi, we conclude that eXi​eXje_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}} is an idempotent as well, and hence p⁡(Xi,Xj)p(X_{i},X_{j}) holds. This proves (iv).

We proved the necessity of the condition stated in the theorem. Now we prove sufficiency. We claim that the elements φ⁡(x1),φ⁡(x2),…,φ⁡(xn)\varphi(x_{1}),\varphi(x_{2}),\dots,\varphi(x_{n}) satisfy the defining relations of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}. Hence, we need to show that eX1,eX2,…,eXne_{X_{1}},e_{X_{2}},\dots,e_{X_{n}} satisfy the defining relations of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}. Let i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n].

Case 1: ii and jj are not connected. We need to show that

eXi​eXj=eXj​eXi.e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}=e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}}.

By assumption, p⁡(Xi,Xj)p(X_{i},X_{j}) and p⁡(Xj,Xi)p(X_{j},X_{i}) hold. By (3), we have Xi∪Xj∈AΘX_{i}\cup X_{j}\in A_{\Theta} and

eXi​eXj=eXi∪XjandeXj​eXi=eXj∪Xi,e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}=e_{X_{i}\cup X_{j}}\quad\text{and}\quad e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}}=e_{X_{j}\cup X_{i}},

and hence

eXi​eXj=eXi∪Xj=eXj∪Xi=eXj​eXi,e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}=e_{X_{i}\cup X_{j}}=e_{X_{j}\cup X_{i}}=e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}},

which we wanted to prove.

Case 2: i→ji\to j. We need to show that

eXi​eXj​eXi=eXj​eXi​eXj=eXi​eXj.e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}}=e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}=e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}.

By assumption, p⁡(Xi,Xj)p(X_{i},X_{j}) holds, and hence eXi​eXje_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}} is an idempotent. Proposition 2.10 implies

eXi​eXj​eXi=eXj​eXi​eXj=eXi​eXj,e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}}=e_{X_{j}}e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}}=e_{X_{i}}e_{X_{j}},

which we wanted to prove.

Hence, the elements φ⁡(x1),φ⁡(x2),…,φ⁡(xn)\varphi(x_{1}),\varphi(x_{2}),\dots,\varphi(x_{n}) satisfy the defining relations of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}, and thus we can extend φ\varphi to a monoid endomorphism of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}. ∎

Denote by

Sn={(X1,X2,…,Xn)∣Xi⊆[n] for i=1,2,…,n},S_{n}=\{(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n})\mid X_{i}\subseteq[n]\text{ for }i=1,2,\dots,n\},

the set of sequences of subsets of [n][n].

Definition 3.2.

A sequence of sets (X1,X2,…,Xn)∈Sn(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n})\in S_{n} is said to be (Θ,p)(\Theta,p)-pure if, for all i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n], the following conditions hold:

  1. (i)

    Xi∈AΘX_{i}\in A_{\Theta};

  2. (ii)

    p⁡(Xi,Xj)p(X_{i},X_{j}) and p⁡(Xj,Xi)p(X_{j},X_{i}) hold if ii and jj are not connected;

  3. (iii)

    p⁡(Xi,Xj)p(X_{i},X_{j}) holds if i→ji\to j.

We also define

Sn​(Θ,p)={(X1,X2,…,Xn)∈Sn∣(X1,X2,…,Xn)​ is (Θ,p)-pure}.S_{n}(\Theta,p)=\{(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n})\in S_{n}\mid(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n})\text{ is $(\Theta,p)$-pure}\}.

Define the map Φ:End⁡(HKΘ)→Sn\Phi:\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta})\to S_{n} by

Φ⁡(φ)=(c⁡(φ⁡(x1)),c⁡(φ⁡(x2)),…,c⁡(φ⁡(xn))).\Phi(\varphi)=\big(c(\varphi(x_{1})),c(\varphi(x_{2})),\dots,c(\varphi(x_{n}))\big).
Theorem 3.3.

The map Φ:End⁡(HKΘ)→Sn​(Θ,p)\Phi:\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta})\to S_{n}(\Theta,p) is a bijection.

Proof.

Let φ∈End⁡(HKΘ)\varphi\in\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}). By Theorem 3.1, there exists a (Θ,p)(\Theta,p)-pure sequence of sets (X1,X2,…,Xn)(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}) such that

φ⁡(xi)=eXi,\varphi(x_{i})=e_{X_{i}},

for all i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\dots,n. Hence,

Φ⁡(φ)=(c⁡(eX1),c⁡(eX2),…,c⁡(eXn))=(X1,X2,…,Xn),\Phi(\varphi)=(c(e_{X_{1}}),c(e_{X_{2}}),\dots,c(e_{X_{n}}))=(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}),

which proves that Φ\Phi maps into Sn​(Θ,p)S_{n}(\Theta,p).

Since every endomorphism of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} is uniquely determined by the images of the generators, since every endomorphism of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} maps generators to idempotents, and since idempotents in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} are uniquely determined by their content, Φ\Phi is injective.

Let (X1,X2,…,Xn)∈Sn​(Θ,p)(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n})\in S_{n}(\Theta,p). Then by Theorem 3.1, the map xi↦eXix_{i}\mapsto e_{X_{i}} extends to an endomorphism φ\varphi of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}. Since c⁡(φ⁡(xi))=c⁡(eXi)=Xic(\varphi(x_{i}))=c(e_{X_{i}})=X_{i} for i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\dots,n, we obtain Φ⁡(φ)=(X1,X2,…,Xn)\Phi(\varphi)=(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}), and hence surjectivity follows. ∎

3.2 The Maps Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi

The following definitions and statements are very similar to the results in Andrenšek (2025). We prove these results again because the results in Andrenšek (2025) were derived for the Kiselman monoid, which is a special case of HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}. For completeness, we include the proofs here for HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}.

For 𝐗∈Sn\mathbf{X}\in S_{n}, denote by 𝐗i\mathbf{X}_{i} the ii-th set of the sequence 𝐗\mathbf{X}. We define the binary operation ∗\ast on SnS_{n} as follows. Let 𝐗=(X1,X2,…,Xn)\mathbf{X}=(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}) and 𝐘=(Y1,Y2,…,Yn)\mathbf{Y}=(Y_{1},Y_{2},\dots,Y_{n}) be elements of SnS_{n}. We define 𝐙=𝐗∗𝐘\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{Y}, where 𝐙=(Z1,Z2,…,Zn)\mathbf{Z}=(Z_{1},Z_{2},\dots,Z_{n}) is given by

Zi=⋃j∈YiXj\displaystyle Z_{i}=\bigcup\limits_{j\in Y_{i}}X_{j}

for all i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\dots,n. It quickly follows that (Sn,∗)(S_{n},\ast) is a monoid with unit element ({1},{2},…,{n})(\{1\},\{2\},\dots,\{n\}).

Theorem 3.4.

The map Φ:End⁡(HKΘ)→Sn\Phi:\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta})\to S_{n} is a homomorphism of monoids from End⁡(HKΘ)\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}) to (Sn,∗)(S_{n},\ast).

Proof.

Let ψ,φ∈End⁡(HKΘ)\psi,\varphi\in\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}) and let i∈[n]i\in[n]. By Lemma 2.1, we have

(Φ⁡(ψ∘φ))i=c⁡((ψ∘φ)​(xi))=⋃j∈c⁡(φ⁡(xi))c⁡(ψ⁡(xj)).(\Phi(\psi\circ\varphi))_{i}=c((\psi\circ\varphi)(x_{i}))=\bigcup_{j\in c(\varphi(x_{i}))}c(\psi(x_{j})).

We also have

(Φ⁡(ψ)∗Φ⁡(φ))i\displaystyle\big(\Phi(\psi)\ast\Phi(\varphi)\big)_{i} =((c⁡(ψ⁡(x1)),…,c⁡(ψ⁡(xn)))∗(c⁡(φ⁡(x1)),…,c⁡(φ⁡(xn))))i\displaystyle=\big((c(\psi(x_{1})),\dots,c(\psi(x_{n})))\ast(c(\varphi(x_{1})),\dots,c(\varphi(x_{n})))\big)_{i}
=⋃j∈c⁡(φ⁡(xi))c⁡(ψ⁡(xj)).\displaystyle=\bigcup_{j\in c(\varphi(x_{i}))}c(\psi(x_{j})).

We thus have

(Φ⁡(ψ∘φ))i=(Φ⁡(ψ)∗Φ⁡(φ))i.\big(\Phi(\psi\circ\varphi)\big)_{i}=\big(\Phi(\psi)\ast\Phi(\varphi)\big)_{i}.

It follows that

Φ⁡(ψ∘φ)=Φ⁡(ψ)∗Φ⁡(φ),\displaystyle\Phi(\psi\circ\varphi)=\Phi(\psi)\ast\Phi(\varphi),

proving that Φ\Phi is multiplicative. Since the identity map is the unit element of End⁡(HKΘ)\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}), and because of

Φ⁡(idHKΘ)=({1},{2},…,{n}),\displaystyle\Phi(\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}})=(\{1\},\{2\},\dots,\{n\}),

we conclude that Φ\Phi is a monoid homomorphism. ∎

Now we denote by BnB_{n} the set of all n×nn\times n Boolean matrices. For A∈BnA\in B_{n} and i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n], denote by Ai,jA_{i,j} the (i,j)(i,j) entry of AA. We define the binary operation ⋅\cdot on BnB_{n} as follows. Let A,B∈BnA,B\in B_{n}. Then C=A⋅BC=A\cdot B, with

Ci,j=⋁k=1n(Ai,k∧Bk,j),\displaystyle C_{i,j}=\bigvee_{k=1}^{n}(A_{i,k}\land B_{k,j}),

for all i,j=1,2,…,ni,j=1,2,\dots,n. Here, ∨\lor denotes the Boolean join and ∧\land denotes the Boolean meet on {0,1}\{0,1\}. One can easily check that (Bn,⋅)(B_{n},\cdot) is a monoid, and its unit element is the identity matrix II of size n×nn\times n.

Theorem 3.5.

The map Ψ:Sn→Bn\Psi:S_{n}\to B_{n}, defined by

Ψ​(𝐗)x,i={1,x∈Xi,0,x∉Xi,\Psi(\mathbf{X})_{x,i}=\begin{cases}1,&x\in X_{i},\\ 0,&x\notin X_{i},\end{cases}

for all x,i=1,2,…,nx,i=1,2,\dots,n, is an isomorphism of monoids from (Sn,∗)(S_{n},\ast) to (Bn,⋅)(B_{n},\cdot).

Proof.

The map Ψ\Psi is obviously bijective.

Now we show that Ψ\Psi is multiplicative. Let 𝐗,𝐘∈Sn\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}\in S_{n}, where 𝐗=(X1,X2,…,Xn)\mathbf{X}=(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}) and 𝐘=(Y1,Y2,…,Yn)\mathbf{Y}=(Y_{1},Y_{2},\dots,Y_{n}). We compute

Ψ⁡(𝐗∗𝐘)=Ψ⁡(⋃j∈Y1Xj,⋃j∈Y2Xj,…,⋃j∈YnXj).\displaystyle\Psi(\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{Y})=\Psi(\bigcup_{j\in Y_{1}}X_{j},\bigcup_{j\in Y_{2}}X_{j},\dots,\bigcup_{j\in Y_{n}}X_{j}).

It follows that for x,i∈[n]x,i\in[n] we have

Ψ​(𝐗∗𝐘)x,i=1\displaystyle\Psi(\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{Y})_{x,i}=1 ⇔x∈⋃j∈YiXj\displaystyle\iff x\in\bigcup_{j\in Y_{i}}X_{j}
⇔there exists ​k∈Yi​ such that ​x∈Xk.\displaystyle\iff\text{there exists }k\in Y_{i}\text{ such that }x\in X_{k}.

On the other hand,

(Ψ⁡(𝐗)⋅Ψ⁡(𝐘))x,i=⋁k=1n(Ψ​(𝐗)x,k∧Ψ​(𝐘)k,i).\displaystyle(\Psi(\mathbf{X})\cdot\Psi(\mathbf{Y}))_{x,i}=\bigvee_{k=1}^{n}(\Psi(\mathbf{X})_{x,k}\land\Psi(\mathbf{Y})_{k,i}).

Hence, we have

(Ψ⁡(𝐗)⋅Ψ⁡(𝐘))x,i=1\displaystyle(\Psi(\mathbf{X})\cdot\Psi(\mathbf{Y}))_{x,i}=1 ⇔there exists ​k∈[n]​ such that ​Ψ​(𝐗)x,k=Ψ​(𝐘)k,i=1\displaystyle\iff\text{there exists }k\in[n]\text{ such that }\Psi(\mathbf{X})_{x,k}=\Psi(\mathbf{Y})_{k,i}=1
⇔there exists ​k∈[n]​ such that ​x∈Xk​ and ​k∈Yi\displaystyle\iff\text{there exists }k\in[n]\text{ such that }x\in X_{k}\text{ and }k\in Y_{i}
⇔there exists ​k∈Yi​ such that ​x∈Xk.\displaystyle\iff\text{there exists }k\in Y_{i}\text{ such that }x\in X_{k}.

We thus obtain

Ψ​(𝐗∗𝐘)x,i=1⇔(Ψ⁡(𝐗)⋅Ψ⁡(𝐘))x,i=1,\Psi(\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{Y})_{x,i}=1\iff(\Psi(\mathbf{X})\cdot\Psi(\mathbf{Y}))_{x,i}=1,

and since Ψ⁡(𝐗∗𝐘)\Psi(\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{Y}) and Ψ⁡(𝐗)⋅Ψ⁡(𝐘)\Psi(\mathbf{X})\cdot\Psi(\mathbf{Y}) are both Boolean matrices, we get

Ψ​(𝐗∗𝐘)x,i=(Ψ⁡(𝐗)⋅Ψ⁡(𝐘))x,i.\Psi(\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{Y})_{x,i}=(\Psi(\mathbf{X})\cdot\Psi(\mathbf{Y}))_{x,i}.

Since xx and ii are arbitrary, it follows that

Ψ⁡(𝐗∗𝐘)=Ψ⁡(𝐗)⋅Ψ⁡(𝐘).\displaystyle\Psi(\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{Y})=\Psi(\mathbf{X})\cdot\Psi(\mathbf{Y}).

Furthermore, since Ψ⁡({1},{2},…,{n})=I\Psi(\{1\},\{2\},\dots,\{n\})=I, it follows that Ψ\Psi is an isomorphism of monoids. ∎

The map Ψ\Psi has a particularly simple interpretation: it encodes, in matrix form, which elements are contained in each set of the sequence. More precisely, if 𝐗=(X1,X2,…,Xn)\mathbf{X}=(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}), then the ii-th column of Ψ⁡(𝐗)\Psi(\mathbf{X}) is the characteristic vector of the set XiX_{i}. Equivalently, for x,i∈[n]x,i\in[n], we have

Ψ​(𝐗)x,i=1⇔x∈Xi.\Psi(\mathbf{X})_{x,i}=1\iff x\in X_{i}.
Theorem 3.6.

The set Sn​(Θ,p)S_{n}(\Theta,p), equipped with the operation ∗\ast, is a monoid and we have

End⁡(HKΘ)≅Sn​(Θ,p)≅Ψ⁡(Sn​(Θ,p)).\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta})\cong S_{n}(\Theta,p)\cong\Psi(S_{n}(\Theta,p)).
Proof.

By Theorem 3.3, Φ:End⁡(HKΘ)→Sn​(Θ,p)\Phi:\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta})\to S_{n}(\Theta,p) is a bijection. Using Theorem 3.4, we conclude that

Φ:End⁡(HKΘ)→(Sn​(Θ,p),∗)\Phi:\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta})\to(S_{n}(\Theta,p),\ast)

is an isomorphism. Since Sn​(Θ,p)S_{n}(\Theta,p) is the image of an isomorphism, it is a monoid for the operation ∗\ast and its unit element is ({1},{2},…,{n})(\{1\},\{2\},\dots,\{n\}). Hence

End⁡(HKΘ)≅Sn​(Θ,p).\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta})\cong S_{n}(\Theta,p).

By Theorem 3.5, the restriction Ψ|Sn​(Θ,p):Sn​(Θ,p)→Bn\Psi|_{S_{n}(\Theta,p)}:S_{n}(\Theta,p)\to B_{n} is a monomorphism of monoids, and hence Ψ|Sn​(Θ,p):Sn​(Θ,p)→Ψ⁡(Sn​(Θ,p))\Psi|_{S_{n}(\Theta,p)}:S_{n}(\Theta,p)\to\Psi(S_{n}(\Theta,p)) is an isomorphism of monoids. We thus get

Sn​(Θ,p)≅Ψ⁡(Sn​(Θ,p)).S_{n}(\Theta,p)\cong\Psi(S_{n}(\Theta,p)).

∎

We summarise the procedure to determine End⁡(HKΘ)\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}) as follows:

  1. (i)

    Determine the set AΘA_{\Theta} of all sets X⊆VX\subseteq V such that Θ⁡[X]\Theta[X] does not contain any oriented cycles and determine all eXe_{X} for X∈AΘX\in A_{\Theta} using Lemma 2.7.

  2. (ii)

    Determine the predicate pp such that p⁡(X,Y)⇔eX​eYp(X,Y)\iff e_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}, for X,Y∈AΘX,Y\in A_{\Theta}.

  3. (iii)

    Determine all (Θ,p)(\Theta,p)-pure sequences of sets from Definition 3.2.

  4. (iv)

    Compute Ψ​(Sn​(Θ,p))\Psi(S_{n}(\Theta,p)) and use Theorem 3.6 to conclude that End⁡(HKΘ)≅Ψ⁡(Sn​(Θ,p))\mathrm{End}(\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta})\cong\Psi(S_{n}(\Theta,p)).

Notice that the last step is trivial, since Ψ\Psi is a very simple map. Moreover, determining AΘA_{\Theta} is not difficult either. The difficult part of this procedure is determining the predicate pp.

We can quickly demonstrate this procedure in the case when HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} is isomorphic to the Kiselman monoid KnK_{n}. In this case, the graph Θ\Theta is acyclic and hence AΘ=𝟚[n]A_{\Theta}=\mathbbm{2}^{[n]}. For a nonempty X={i1,i2,…,ik}⊆[n]X=\{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k}\}\subseteq[n] with i1<i2<⋯<iki_{1}<i_{2}<\dots<i_{k}, we have that ij→ij′i_{j}\to i_{j^{\prime}} implies j>j′j>j^{\prime}. Hence, the unique idempotent with content XX is ϵX\epsilon_{X}.

In Proposition 2.2, it is shown that the predicate pp in KnK_{n} is given by

p⁡(X,Y)⇔∀x∈X∖Y,∀y∈Y∖X:x>y.p(X,Y)\iff\forall x\in X\setminus Y,\forall y\in Y\setminus X:x>y.

Hence, a sequence (X1,X2,…,Xn)(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}) is (Θ,p)(\Theta,p)-pure if and only if for i>ji>j, we have p⁡(Xi,Xj)p(X_{i},X_{j}). These are the so-called monotone sequences as defined in (Andrenšek, 2025, Definition 3). In that paper, the endomorphism monoid of KnK_{n} is shown to be isomorphic to a submonoid of BnB_{n} of matrices avoiding a certain pattern. They denote this monoid by DnD_{n}. It quickly follows that Ψ​(Sn​(Θ,p))\Psi(S_{n}(\Theta,p)) coincides with DnD_{n}.

4 Endomorphisms of the Catalan Monoid

In this section, we determine all endomorphisms of the Catalan monoid. We follow the procedure established in Section 3.

In (Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk, 2011, Theorem 1(viii)), it is shown that, in this case, HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} is isomorphic to the Catalan monoid 𝒞n+1\mathcal{C}_{n+1}. The Catalan monoid 𝒞n+1\mathcal{C}_{n+1} is the monoid of all order-preserving and order-decreasing total transformations of the set [n+1][n+1]. That is, the set of all f:[n+1]→[n+1]f:[n+1]\to[n+1] such that:

  1. (i)

    f⁡(i)≤f⁡(j)f(i)\leq f(j) for i,j∈[n+1]i,j\in[n+1] with i≤ji\leq j (order-preserving);

  2. (ii)

    f⁡(i)≤if(i)\leq i for i∈[n+1]i\in[n+1] (order-decreasing).

The operation in 𝒞n+1\mathcal{C}_{n+1} is the usual composition and the unit element is the identity on [n+1][n+1]. For f,g∈𝒞n+1f,g\in\mathcal{C}_{n+1}, we denote by f​g=f∘gfg=f\circ g.

Catalan monoids and their presentations were studied in Solomon (1996). In (Stanley, 1999, 6.25(g)), it was shown that |𝒞n+1|=Cn+1|\mathcal{C}_{n+1}|=C_{n+1}, where Cn=1n+1​(2​nn)C_{n}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n} denotes the nn-th Catalan number.

In the proof of (Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk, 2011, Theorem 1(vii)), the authors use the fact that the transformations TiT_{i} for i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\dots,n, defined by

Ti​(j)={i,j=i+1,j,otherwise,T_{i}(j)=\begin{cases}i,&j=i+1,\\ j,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

generate 𝒞n+1\mathcal{C}_{n+1}. The corresponding isomorphism of monoids from HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} to 𝒞n+1\mathcal{C}_{n+1} is then given by the unique extension of the mapping xi↦Tix_{i}\mapsto T_{i} and we denote it by τ\tau.

Step 1: Determine AΘA_{\Theta} and idempotents

Since Θ\Theta is acyclic, we have AΘ=𝟚[n]A_{\Theta}=\mathbbm{2}^{[n]}. For nonempty X={i1,i2,…,ik}⊆[n]X=\{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k}\}\subseteq[n] with i1>i2>⋯>iki_{1}>i_{2}>\dots>i_{k}, we have that ij→ij′i_{j}\to i_{j^{\prime}} implies j>j′j>j^{\prime}. By Lemma 2.7, we have

eX=xik​…​xi2​xi1.e_{X}=x_{i_{k}}\dots x_{i_{2}}x_{i_{1}}. (4)

Hence, in this case, idempotents are written as products in which the indices of the generators increase from left to right. Observe that in the Kiselman monoid, we have the converse case. We also denote TX=τ⁡(eX)T_{X}=\tau(e_{X}). In particular, T∅T_{\emptyset} is the identity on [n+1][n+1].

Since τ\tau is an isomorphism of monoids, eX​eYe_{X}e_{Y} is an idempotent in HKΘ\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta} if and only if TX​TYT_{X}T_{Y} is an idempotent in 𝒞n+1\mathcal{C}_{n+1} and eX​eY=eX∪Ye_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y} if and only if TX​TY=TX∪YT_{X}T_{Y}=T_{X\cup Y}. By (3), we then have

p⁡(X,Y)⇔eX​eY​ is an idempotent⇔TX​TY​ is an idempotent⇔TX​TY=TX∪Y.p(X,Y)\iff e_{X}e_{Y}\text{ is an idempotent}\iff T_{X}T_{Y}\text{ is an idempotent}\iff T_{X}T_{Y}=T_{X\cup Y}. (5)

Step 2: Determine the predicate pp

For X⊆[n]X\subseteq[n], define the following set

FX=[n+1]∖{x+1∣x∈X}.F_{X}=[n+1]\setminus\{x+1\mid x\in X\}.

Note that 1∈FX1\in F_{X} for any X⊆[n]X\subseteq[n]. For a∈[n+1]a\in[n+1], we have

a∈FX⇔a−1∉X.a\in F_{X}\iff a-1\notin X. (6)

For any X,Y⊆[n]X,Y\subseteq[n], we also have

FX∪Y=FX∩FY.F_{X\cup Y}=F_{X}\cap F_{Y}. (7)
Proposition 4.1.

Let X⊆[n]X\subseteq[n]. Then we have

TX​(t)=max⁡(FX∩[t]),T_{X}(t)=\max(F_{X}\cap[t]),

for all t∈[n+1]t\in[n+1].

Proof.

We prove the formula by induction on |X||X|. If X=∅X=\emptyset, then we have FX=[n+1]F_{X}=[n+1]. Hence FX∩[t]=[t]F_{X}\cap[t]=[t] for all t∈[n+1]t\in[n+1]. Since TXT_{X} is the identity on [n+1][n+1], we indeed have

TX​(t)=t=max⁡([t])=max⁡(FX∩[t]).T_{X}(t)=t=\max([t])=\max(F_{X}\cap[t]).

Let |X|=r|X|=r with 0<r≤n0<r\leq n and assume that the formula in the statement holds for all sets Y⊆[n]Y\subseteq[n] with |Y|<r|Y|<r. Write XX as

X={i1,i2,…,ir−1,ir}X=\{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{r-1},i_{r}\}

with i1<i2<⋯<ir−1<iri_{1}<i_{2}<\dots<i_{r-1}<i_{r}. Denote by Y=X∖{ir}Y=X\setminus\{i_{r}\}. Then |Y|=r−1|Y|=r-1 and by the induction hypothesis, we have

TY​(t)=max⁡(FY∩[t]).T_{Y}(t)=\max(F_{Y}\cap[t]).

By the definition of TXT_{X} and (4), we have TX=TY​TirT_{X}=T_{Y}T_{i_{r}}. Hence

TX​(t)=(TY∘Tir)​(t)=TY​(Tir​(t))=max⁡(FY∩[Tir​(t)]).T_{X}(t)=(T_{Y}\circ T_{i_{r}})(t)=T_{Y}(T_{i_{r}}(t))=\max(F_{Y}\cap[T_{i_{r}}(t)]).

Observe that

FX=FY∪{ir}=FY∩F{ir}=FY∖{ir+1}.F_{X}=F_{Y\cup\{i_{r}\}}=F_{Y}\cap F_{\{i_{r}\}}=F_{Y}\setminus\{i_{r}+1\}.

Now we consider different cases on the value of t∈[n+1]t\in[n+1].

Case 1: t<ir+1t<i_{r}+1. In this case, we have Tir​(t)=tT_{i_{r}}(t)=t. We also have

[t]=[t]∖{ir+1}.[t]=[t]\setminus\{i_{r}+1\}.

Hence

FY∩[Tir​(t)]=FY∩[t]=FY∩([t]∖{ir+1})=(FY∖{ir+1})∩[t]=FX∩[t].F_{Y}\cap[T_{i_{r}}(t)]=F_{Y}\cap[t]=F_{Y}\cap([t]\setminus\{i_{r}+1\})=(F_{Y}\setminus\{i_{r}+1\})\cap[t]=F_{X}\cap[t].

Thus,

TX​(t)=max⁡(FY∩[Tir​(t)])=max⁡(FX∩[t]).T_{X}(t)=\max(F_{Y}\cap[T_{i_{r}}(t)])=\max(F_{X}\cap[t]).

Case 2: t=ir+1t=i_{r}+1. In this case, we have Tir​(t)=irT_{i_{r}}(t)=i_{r} and also

[ir]=[ir]∖{ir+1}.[i_{r}]=[i_{r}]\setminus\{i_{r}+1\}.

Hence

FY∩[Tir​(t)]=FY∩[ir]=FY∩([ir]∖{ir+1})=(FY∖{ir+1})∩[ir]=FX∩[ir].F_{Y}\cap[T_{i_{r}}(t)]=F_{Y}\cap[i_{r}]=F_{Y}\cap([i_{r}]\setminus\{i_{r}+1\})=(F_{Y}\setminus\{i_{r}+1\})\cap[i_{r}]=F_{X}\cap[i_{r}].

Since ir+1∉FXi_{r}+1\notin F_{X}, we have

FX∩[ir+1]=FX∩([ir]∪{ir+1})=(FX∩[ir])∪(FX∩{ir+1})=(FX∩[ir])∪∅=FX∩[ir].F_{X}\cap[i_{r}+1]=F_{X}\cap([i_{r}]\cup\{i_{r}+1\})=(F_{X}\cap[i_{r}])\cup(F_{X}\cap\{i_{r}+1\})=(F_{X}\cap[i_{r}])\cup\emptyset=F_{X}\cap[i_{r}].

Thus we obtain

FY∩[Tir​(t)]=FX∩[ir]=FX∩[ir+1]=FX∩[t].F_{Y}\cap[T_{i_{r}}(t)]=F_{X}\cap[i_{r}]=F_{X}\cap[i_{r}+1]=F_{X}\cap[t].

Therefore, we again conclude

TX​(t)=max⁡(FY∩[Tir​(t)])=max⁡(FX∩[t]).T_{X}(t)=\max(F_{Y}\cap[T_{i_{r}}(t)])=\max(F_{X}\cap[t]).

Case 3: t>ir+1t>i_{r}+1. Since i1<i2<⋯<ir<ir+1<ti_{1}<i_{2}<\dots<i_{r}<i_{r}+1<t, we obtain ij+1<ti_{j}+1<t for every j=1,2,…,rj=1,2,\dots,r. Hence Tij​(t)=tT_{i_{j}}(t)=t for all j=1,2,…,rj=1,2,\dots,r. Thus,

TX​(t)=(Ti1​Ti2​…​Tir)​(t)=t,T_{X}(t)=(T_{i_{1}}T_{i_{2}}\dots T_{i_{r}})(t)=t,

since each TijT_{i_{j}} fixes tt. On the other hand, since t−1>ir=max⁡Xt-1>i_{r}=\max X, we have t−1∉Xt-1\notin X, and hence (6) implies t∈FXt\in F_{X}. It follows that

max⁡(FX∩[t])=t,\max(F_{X}\cap[t])=t,

which implies

TX​(t)=t=max⁡(FX∩[t]).T_{X}(t)=t=\max(F_{X}\cap[t]).

Hence, for all t∈[n+1]t\in[n+1], we have

TX​(t)=max⁡(FX∩[t]).T_{X}(t)=\max(F_{X}\cap[t]).

This concludes the induction step and hence the proof is finished. ∎

For f:[n+1]→[n+1]f:[n+1]\to[n+1], denote by

Im⁡(f)={f⁡(i)∣i∈[n+1]}andFix⁡(f)={i∈[n+1]∣f⁡(i)=i},\mathrm{Im}(f)=\{f(i)\mid i\in[n+1]\}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{Fix}(f)=\{i\in[n+1]\mid f(i)=i\},

the range of ff and the set of fixed points of ff.

Corollary 4.2.

Let X⊆[n]X\subseteq[n]. Then Im⁡(TX)=Fix⁡(TX)=FX\mathrm{Im}(T_{X})=\mathrm{Fix}(T_{X})=F_{X}.

Proof.

By Proposition 4.1, we have

TX​(t)=t⇔max⁡(FX∩[t])=t⇔t∈FX,T_{X}(t)=t\iff\max(F_{X}\cap[t])=t\iff t\in F_{X},

for t∈[n+1]t\in[n+1]. Hence Fix⁡(TX)=FX\mathrm{Fix}(T_{X})=F_{X}. Since FX∩[t]⊆FXF_{X}\cap[t]\subseteq F_{X} for t∈[n+1]t\in[n+1], Proposition 4.1 implies

TX​(t)=max⁡(FX∩[t])∈FX,T_{X}(t)=\max(F_{X}\cap[t])\in F_{X},

for all t∈[n+1]t\in[n+1], which implies Im⁡(TX)⊆FX\mathrm{Im}(T_{X})\subseteq F_{X}. Since t=TX​(t)∈Im⁡(TX)t=T_{X}(t)\in\mathrm{Im}(T_{X}) for all t∈FXt\in F_{X}, we get FX⊆Im⁡(TX)F_{X}\subseteq\mathrm{Im}(T_{X}), and hence Im⁡(TX)=FX\mathrm{Im}(T_{X})=F_{X}. ∎

Lemma 4.3.

Let f∈𝒞n+1f\in\mathcal{C}_{n+1}. Then ff is an idempotent if and only if Im⁡(f)⊆Fix⁡(f)\mathrm{Im}(f)\subseteq\mathrm{Fix}(f).

Proof.

Assume that ff is an idempotent, that is, f​f=f∘f=fff=f\circ f=f. Then for any f⁡(x)∈Im⁡(f)f(x)\in\mathrm{Im}(f), we have

f⁡(f⁡(x))=(f∘f)​(x)=f⁡(x),f(f(x))=(f\circ f)(x)=f(x),

proving Im⁡(f)⊆Fix⁡(f)\mathrm{Im}(f)\subseteq\mathrm{Fix}(f).

Conversely, suppose Im⁡(f)⊆Fix⁡(f)\mathrm{Im}(f)\subseteq\mathrm{Fix}(f). Pick any x∈[n+1]x\in[n+1]. Then f⁡(x)∈Im⁡(f)f(x)\in\mathrm{Im}(f), and hence f⁡(x)∈Fix⁡(f)f(x)\in\mathrm{Fix}(f). Therefore,

(f​f)​(x)=(f∘f)​(x)=f⁡(f⁡(x))=f⁡(x),(ff)(x)=(f\circ f)(x)=f(f(x))=f(x),

which proves f​f=fff=f, and hence ff is an idempotent. ∎

Theorem 4.4.

Let X,Y⊆[n]X,Y\subseteq[n]. Then

TX​TY​ is an idempotent in ​𝒞n+1⇔TX​(FY)⊆FY.T_{X}T_{Y}\text{ is an idempotent in }\mathcal{C}_{n+1}\iff T_{X}(F_{Y})\subseteq F_{Y}.
Proof.

Assume that TX​TYT_{X}T_{Y} is an idempotent. Then TX​TY=TX∪YT_{X}T_{Y}=T_{X\cup Y} by (5). Then by Corollary 4.2 and (7), we have

Im⁡(TX​TY)=Im⁡(TX∪Y)=FX∪Y=FX∩FY⊆FY.\mathrm{Im}(T_{X}T_{Y})=\mathrm{Im}(T_{X\cup Y})=F_{X\cup Y}=F_{X}\cap F_{Y}\subseteq F_{Y}.

Moreover, by Corollary 4.2, we have

Im⁡(TX​TY)=TX​(Im⁡(TY))=TX​(FY).\mathrm{Im}(T_{X}T_{Y})=T_{X}(\mathrm{Im}(T_{Y}))=T_{X}(F_{Y}).

This implies

TX​(FY)⊆FY,T_{X}(F_{Y})\subseteq F_{Y},

which proves the desired implication.

Suppose TX​(FY)⊆FYT_{X}(F_{Y})\subseteq F_{Y}. By Corollary 4.2, we have FX=Im⁡(TX)F_{X}=\mathrm{Im}(T_{X}). Since TX​(FY)⊆Im⁡(TX)T_{X}(F_{Y})\subseteq\mathrm{Im}(T_{X}), it follows that

TX​(FY)=TX​(FY)∩Im⁡(TX)=TX​(FY)∩FX⊆FY∩FX.T_{X}(F_{Y})=T_{X}(F_{Y})\cap\mathrm{Im}(T_{X})=T_{X}(F_{Y})\cap F_{X}\subseteq F_{Y}\cap F_{X}.

Then again by Corollary 4.2, we obtain

Im⁡(TX​TY)=TX​(Im⁡(TY))=TX​(FY)⊆FX∩FY=Fix⁡(TX)∩Fix⁡(TY)⊆Fix⁡(TX​TY),\mathrm{Im}(T_{X}T_{Y})=T_{X}(\mathrm{Im}(T_{Y}))=T_{X}(F_{Y})\subseteq F_{X}\cap F_{Y}=\mathrm{Fix}(T_{X})\cap\mathrm{Fix}(T_{Y})\subseteq\mathrm{Fix}(T_{X}T_{Y}),

since Fix⁡(TX)∩Fix⁡(TY)⊆Fix⁡(TX​TY)\mathrm{Fix}(T_{X})\cap\mathrm{Fix}(T_{Y})\subseteq\mathrm{Fix}(T_{X}T_{Y}); if TX​(z)=zT_{X}(z)=z and TY​(z)=zT_{Y}(z)=z, then (TX​TY)​(z)=TX​(TY​(z))=TX​(z)=z(T_{X}T_{Y})(z)=T_{X}(T_{Y}(z))=T_{X}(z)=z. By Lemma 4.3, TX​TYT_{X}T_{Y} is an idempotent. ∎

Theorem 4.5.

We have

p⁡(X,Y)⇔∀a∈[n+1]:a−1∉Y⇒max⁡([a]∖{x+1∣x∈X})−1∉Y.p(X,Y)\iff\forall a\in[n+1]:a-1\notin Y\Rightarrow\max([a]\setminus\{x+1\mid x\in X\})-1\notin Y.
Proof.

By Theorem 4.4, TX​TYT_{X}T_{Y} is an idempotent if and only if TX​(FY)⊆FYT_{X}(F_{Y})\subseteq F_{Y}. We have

TX​(FY)⊆FY⇔∀a∈FY:TX​(a)∈FY.T_{X}(F_{Y})\subseteq F_{Y}\iff\forall a\in F_{Y}:T_{X}(a)\in F_{Y}.

By (6), this is equivalent to

∀a∈[n+1]:a−1∉Y⇒TX​(a)−1∉Y.\forall a\in[n+1]:a-1\notin Y\Rightarrow T_{X}(a)-1\notin Y.

Moreover, by Proposition 4.1, for a∈[n+1]a\in[n+1], we have

TX​(a)=max⁡(FX∩[a])=max⁡(([n+1]∖{x+1∣x∈X})∩[a])=max⁡([a]∖{x+1∣x∈X}).T_{X}(a)=\max(F_{X}\cap[a])=\max(([n+1]\setminus\{x+1\mid x\in X\})\cap[a])=\max([a]\setminus\{x+1\mid x\in X\}).

Thus,

TX​TY​ is an idempotent⇔∀a∈[n+1]:a−1∉Y⇒max⁡([a]∖{x+1∣x∈X})−1∉Y.T_{X}T_{Y}\text{ is an idempotent}\iff\forall a\in[n+1]:a-1\notin Y\Rightarrow\max([a]\setminus\{x+1\mid x\in X\})-1\notin Y.

The conclusion of the theorem follows from (5). ∎

In principle, we have now determined pp. We now try to write the predicate in simpler terms. For a,b∈[n]a,b\in[n] with a≤ba\leq b, we write [a,b][a,b] to denote all i∈[n]i\in[n] such that a≤i≤ba\leq i\leq b. We can write any X⊆[n]X\subseteq[n] as a disjoint union of maximal intervals, that is,

X=⋃i=1k[ai,bi],X=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}[a_{i},b_{i}],

such that the union is disjoint and bi+1<ai+1b_{i}+1<a_{i+1} for i=1,2,…,k−1i=1,2,\dots,k-1.

Lemma 4.6.

Let X,Y⊆[n]X,Y\subseteq[n]. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    p⁡(X,Y)p(X,Y) holds.

  2. (ii)

    For every maximal interval [a,b][a,b] of XX, the following implication holds:

    a−1∈Y⇒[a,b]⊆Y.a-1\in Y\Rightarrow[a,b]\subseteq Y.
Proof.

(i) ⇒\Rightarrow (ii). Let [a,b][a,b] be a maximal interval of XX such that

a−1∈Y.a-1\in Y. (8)

We show [a,b]⊆Y[a,b]\subseteq Y. Suppose there exists c∈[a,b]c\in[a,b] such that c∉Yc\notin Y. Since X⊆[n]X\subseteq[n], we have c+1∈[n+1]c+1\in[n+1]. Then

(c+1)−1=c∉Y,(c+1)-1=c\notin Y,

and since p⁡(X,Y)p(X,Y) holds, by Theorem 4.5, we have

max⁡([c+1]∖{x+1∣x∈X})−1∉Y.\max([c+1]\setminus\{x+1\mid x\in X\})-1\notin Y. (9)

Since [a,b][a,b] is a maximal interval of XX and c∈[a,b]c\in[a,b], we have

max⁡([c+1]∖{x+1∣x∈X})=a,\max([c+1]\setminus\{x+1\mid x\in X\})=a,

and hence (9) implies

a−1∉Y.a-1\notin Y.

This contradicts (8). We reached a contradiction, and hence we must have [a,b]⊆Y[a,b]\subseteq Y.

(ii) ⇒\Rightarrow (i). Let a∈[n+1]a\in[n+1] with a−1∉Ya-1\notin Y. By Theorem 4.5, to prove p⁡(X,Y)p(X,Y), it suffices to show that for

m=max⁡([a]∖{x+1∣x∈X}),m=\max([a]\setminus\{x+1\mid x\in X\}),

we have m−1∉Ym-1\notin Y. If a=1a=1, then m=1m=1 and we have m−1∉Ym-1\notin Y. Suppose a>1a>1. If m=1m=1 or m=am=a, then m−1∉Ym-1\notin Y. Now assume 1<m<a1<m<a and suppose m−1∈Ym-1\in Y. We now construct a contradiction. By the definition of mm, we have m∈[a]m\in[a], m−1∉Xm-1\notin X, and

m+1,m+2,…,a∈{x+1∣x∈X},m+1,m+2,\dots,a\in\{x+1\mid x\in X\},

which implies

m,m+1,…,a−1∈X.m,m+1,\dots,a-1\in X.

Therefore,

[m,a−1]⊆Xandm−1∉X.[m,a-1]\subseteq X\quad\text{and}\quad m-1\notin X.

Hence, some maximal interval of XX starts in mm and we denote this maximal interval of XX by [m,b][m,b] for some b≥a−1b\geq a-1. By the condition (ii) and the assumption that m−1∈Ym-1\in Y, we have [m,b]⊆Y[m,b]\subseteq Y. Since b≥a−1b\geq a-1, we get a−1∈Ya-1\in Y, which contradicts a−1∉Ya-1\notin Y. Therefore, m−1∉Ym-1\notin Y, and p⁡(X,Y)p(X,Y) indeed holds. ∎

This lemma gives an intuitive description of pp.

Step 3: Determine (Θ,p)(\Theta,p)-pure sequences of sets

Since we only have edges i→i+1i\to i+1 for i=1,…,n−1i=1,\dots,n-1 in Θ\Theta and AΘ=𝟚[n]A_{\Theta}=\mathbbm{2}^{[n]}, a sequence of sets (X1,X2,…,Xn)∈Sn(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n})\in S_{n} is (Θ,p)(\Theta,p)-pure if and only if

  1. (i)

    p⁡(Xi,Xj)p(X_{i},X_{j}) and p⁡(Xj,Xi)p(X_{j},X_{i}) hold if |i−j|>1|i-j|>1,

  2. (ii)

    p⁡(Xi,Xi+1)p(X_{i},X_{i+1}) holds for i=1,2,…,n−1i=1,2,\dots,n-1.

These two conditions imply that p⁡(Xi,Xj)p(X_{i},X_{j}) holds for all distinct i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n], except perhaps not in the case when j=i−1j=i-1. Hence (X1,X2,…,Xn)∈Sn(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n})\in S_{n} is (Θ,p)(\Theta,p)-pure if and only if

i≠j+1⇒p⁡(Xi,Xj),i\neq j+1\Rightarrow p(X_{i},X_{j}),

holds for all distinct i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n].

Step 4: Compute Ψ​(Sn​(Θ,p))\Psi(S_{n}(\Theta,p))

We can write Ψ​(Sn​(Θ,p))\Psi(S_{n}(\Theta,p)) as

Ψ(Sn(Θ,p))={Ψ(X1,X2,…,Xn)∣Xi⊆[n] for i∈[n],∀i,j∈[n]:i≠j,i≠j+1⇒p(Xi,Xj)}.\Psi(S_{n}(\Theta,p))=\{\Psi(X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n})\mid X_{i}\subseteq[n]\text{ for }i\in[n],\forall i,j\in[n]:i\neq j,i\neq j+1\Rightarrow p(X_{i},X_{j})\}. (10)

We now obtain a concrete Boolean matrix monoid that is isomorphic to End⁡(𝒞n+1)\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{C}_{n+1}). By Theorem 3.6, Lemma 4.6, and (10), we have

Theorem 4.7.

Let nn be a positive integer. Then End⁡(𝒞n+1)\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{C}_{n+1}) is isomorphic to

{Ψ(𝐗)∣if i≠j,i≠j+1, and [a,b] is a maximal interval of 𝐗i with a−1∈𝐗j, then [a,b]⊆𝐗j},\{\Psi(\mathbf{X})\mid\text{if }i\neq j,i\neq j+1,\text{ and }[a,b]\text{ is a maximal interval of }\mathbf{X}_{i}\text{ with }a-1\in\mathbf{X}_{j}\text{, then }[a,b]\subseteq\mathbf{X}_{j}\},

equipped with the binary operation ⋅\cdot.

It is understood that in Theorem 4.7, 𝐗∈Sn\mathbf{X}\in S_{n} and i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n].
